speaker: Albert Gu
title: No Priors Ep. 70 | With Cartesia Co-Founders Karan Goel & Albert Gu
question: In long-context model architecture design, why do hybrid models combining mostly recurrent layers with sparse attention layers outperform either pure architecture?
guest: One of the big advantages of recurrent state-space alternatives is linear scaling: the time it takes to process any new token is basically constant time, whereas for a Transformer it scales with the history you've seen. But it is actually a bit of a no-free-lunch thing. The fact that the Transformer is taking longer to process things also means there are things it's better at modeling. We think of state-space models as fuzzy compressors, and maybe the bulk of the processing should be done there. At the same time, it benefits from having some exact retrieval or cache, and that's exactly what a Transformer is. It's literally remembering every single token it's seen, and you're allowed to look back over all of it. That's why it's a lot slower, which can be useful, but probably shouldn't be what the bulk of your model is doing—just like a stateful real-time processing unit augmented with a scratchpad or lookup ability. These ideas are quite synergistic, and combining them into hybrid models works better than either individually. People have independently found that the optimal ratio tends to be mostly SSM layers with a little bit of attention, maybe a ratio of ten to one.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Hybrids win because recurrent (state-space) layers and attention have complementary strengths and failure modes, and a small amount of attention is enough to patch the recurrent weakness.

Recurrent layers such as Mamba, xLSTM, or RWKV compress the entire history into a fixed-size state. That makes them linear-time, constant-memory at inference, and good at summarising, tracking running state, and modelling smooth long-range structure. But the fixed state is a lossy bottleneck: they struggle with exact retrieval, copying, and in-context lookup of arbitrary earlier tokens, and this capacity limit worsens as context grows.

Attention has the opposite profile. It keeps every token accessible and retrieves precisely by content, but costs quadratic compute and a growing cache, and it uses that expensive machinery even for work that simple recurrence handles well.

Since most layers are doing compression and feature-building rather than precise lookup, a few attention layers interleaved among many recurrent ones restore exact recall at a fraction of the cost. Empirical studies (Jamba, Samba, Zamba, MambaFormer, Nvidia's Hymba) find ratios around one attention layer per six or seven recurrent layers match or beat both pure designs on quality per unit compute.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Pure long-context architectures face opposing bottlenecks. Pure recurrent models, such as state-space models and linear RNNs, compress history into a fixed-size state, achieving linear compute and constant memory per token, but inevitably losing fine-grained details needed for exact copying, needle-in-a-haystack lookup, and associative recall. Conversely, pure full-attention Transformers preserve lossless token-level access via a growing KV cache, but incur quadratic compute, severe memory-bandwidth costs, and weaker sequential state-tracking biases, while pure sparse attention drops information between attended positions.

Hybrid architectures outperform both through specialization and synergy. Their recurrent majority cheaply handles local dependencies, sequential state tracking, and continuous global compression without inflating the KV cache. Freed from routine context propagation, the sparse attention layers specialize in precise random-access retrieval over long distances. Simultaneously, recurrence bridges the gaps in sparse attention patterns and builds order-aware contextual representations that sharpen attention queries and keys, yielding stronger recall, reasoning, and hardware efficiency than either pure design.

noweb.answer:
Pure architectures face a fundamental trade-off between compression and exact retrieval. Recurrent and state-space layers process sequences in linear time with a constant-size state, excelling at sequential state tracking and global summarization, but their fixed memory bottleneck makes exact copying and associative recall across long contexts lossy. Conversely, pure attention models rely on a growing key-value cache for lossless random access, incurring heavy compute and memory overhead alongside weaker state-tracking inductive biases.

Hybrid models outperform both through a complementary division of labor. Most layers are recurrent, cheaply handling local context, state evolution, and sequence compression at constant memory cost, while sparse attention layers provide targeted, exact token-to-token lookup across distant positions without maintaining a dense key-value cache throughout the network. Freed from routine local aggregation and positional bookkeeping, attention heads specialize sharply in long-range retrieval and in-context learning. Together, this synergy cures the recall bottlenecks of pure recurrence while slashing memory bandwidth and compute costs relative to pure Transformers, delivering higher accuracy and throughput under fixed resource budgets.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Hybrids work because the two layer types fail in complementary ways.

Recurrent or state-space layers, such as Mamba, linear attention and Gated DeltaNet, squeeze the whole history into a fixed-size state. That keeps compute linear and memory constant, and they handle local patterns well. The cost is that the state is lossy. Both theory and experiments show these layers struggle to recall or copy an exact earlier token, which is the "needle" or associative-recall problem (see Zoology and "Repeat After Me").

Attention keeps every token in its KV cache and can look any of them up exactly. But its compute grows quadratically with length and its cache grows linearly, so long contexts get expensive.

Experiments suggest only a small fraction of layers, often one in four to one in eight, need exact lookup. Those can be attention layers that act as precise retrieval heads, while the recurrent layers cheaply handle most of the sequence mixing and supply positional and local context. That lets attention specialize and often improves performance on contexts longer than those seen in training. Jamba, Samba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next report that, at equal compute, this mix matches or beats pure Transformers on quality and pure recurrent models on recall. It also needs far less memory than a full Transformer. The ratio and where the attention layers go still matter.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Pure recurrent and pure attention architectures suffer from complementary bottlenecks at long context lengths. Recurrent models, such as state-space models and linear attention, compress past context into a fixed-size state. This delivers linear scaling, constant inference memory, and strong local sequence tracking, but the fixed state creates an information bottleneck that degrades exact recall, copying, and in-context retrieval. Conversely, pure Transformers retain every token in a growing key-value cache, enabling sharp long-range lookup, yet incur quadratic prefill compute and severe memory-bandwidth overhead from massive caches.

Hybrid designs resolve this trade-off through specialization. Mostly recurrent layers cheaply handle local mixing, syntactic structure, and state tracking, cutting KV-cache memory and latency by a large factor. Sparse interleaved attention layers act as global random-access pathways, bypassing the recurrent bottleneck whenever exact retrieval or distant cross-referencing is required. Together, they achieve better quality per flop and per byte than either pure architecture alone.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Recurrent layers process long sequences efficiently by carrying forward a fixed-size state. That state can preserve useful summaries, but it can lose specific details that a later token needs. A few attention layers give the model direct access to earlier token representations, making it easier to retrieve a name, copy a value, or connect distant parts of the context.

The hybrid gets most of its sequence processing from efficient recurrent layers and pays the cost of full attention at only a few depths. This can improve long-context recall over a purely recurrent model while reducing computation and key-value cache memory compared with a Transformer that uses attention in every layer. The advantage is a better quality–cost trade-off, and its size depends on the task and where the attention layers are placed.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Recurrent layers and attention layers solve different memory problems. A recurrent layer updates a fixed-size state as it reads, so it can track patterns across a long sequence at low cost. But that state compresses the past. If a later question hinges on an exact name or number, the model may already have discarded it. An attention layer can look back at individual token representations and retrieve the detail when it becomes relevant.

Placing attention in just a few layers gives the model repeated opportunities to retrieve details and carry them forward through the recurrent layers. Compared with pure recurrence, the hybrid improves selective recall. Compared with full attention in every layer, it spends less compute and cache memory on looking back. The advantage is a better balance of accuracy and cost on long contexts, especially when most tokens need only update the running state and a few require precise recall.
